questions.prompt: A new WPF project gives you a Window defined in XAML plus a C# code-behind file. Why does the lesson call this split fundamental?
options: XAML compiles faster than C#, so the window appears sooner at startup
The XAML file is only used by the designer and is thrown away when the app runs
The split is required so the same app can also run on .NET Framework 4.x
It splits layout from behavior, so designers and developers work in parallel
questions.explanation: XAML defines the UI layout and C# defines the behavior; the lesson says this split reduces coupling and lets designers and developers work in parallel.

questions.prompt: How do WinForms and WPF differ in how they render the UI?
options: WinForms uses DirectX (vector-based); WPF uses GDI+ (pixel-based)
WinForms uses GDI+ (pixel-based); WPF uses DirectX (vector-based)
Both use GDI+, but WPF adds a DPI-scaling layer on top
Both use DirectX; WPF just has more built-in controls
questions.explanation: The comparison table lists WinForms rendering as GDI+ (pixel-based, on the CPU) and WPF as DirectX (vector-based, on the GPU), which is why WPF scales well on high-DPI screens.

questions.prompt: In WPF, the Save button is written as `<Button Content="Save" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" />`. Where does its behavior come from?
options: From a `Click` event handler the designer generates in code-behind
From the `Content` property, which WPF maps to a method name
From the binding to `SaveCommand`, not from an event handler
questions.explanation: In WPF the UI is written in XAML and behavior comes from binding (here to `SaveCommand`), not from events, which keeps UI and logic cleanly separated.

questions.prompt: WinForms code sets `textBox1.Text = user.Name;`. What does WPF's `<TextBox Text="{Binding UserName}" />` give you instead?
options: Automatic two-way updates with minimal glue code
A one-time copy of `UserName` when the window loads
Faster rendering, but you still update `Text` manually
Validation of `UserName`, but no automatic updates
questions.explanation: WinForms needs manual updates everywhere, while WPF data binding gives automatic updates, two-way binding and minimal glue code.

questions.prompt: You must keep maintaining a small legacy CRUD tool used internally, and time is extremely limited. Which framework does the lesson suggest?
options: WPF, because it is always the better choice for new work
WPF, because it has built-in animations
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends WinForms for very small apps, legacy maintenance, simple CRUD internal tools and extremely limited time; WPF is for new, medium/large, long-lived or rich-UI apps.
